###### suggestion
Let me describe current situation briefly. We have marker providers which push their markers to markerService. Markers land in 2-d storage divided by `owner`, which is a language sign, and `resource`, which is uri (or its path). This is fine until we get into situation when more that one marker provider manages markers of the same owner+resource, such as in `typescript-language-features` extension and `tsc problem-matcher`. This makes a collision, where one may overwrite each other markers inside markerService, and as it seems to me, it is the main reason of making [WatchingProblemCollector](https://github.com/microsoft/vscode/blob/a5914335df0bf1cae7d818a168ef321def9f8572/src/vs/workbench/contrib/tasks/common/problemCollectors.ts#L412) to repush markers on textModel dispose, and also along with [StartStopProblemCollector](https://github.com/microsoft/vscode/blob/a5914335df0bf1cae7d818a168ef321def9f8572/src/vs/workbench/contrib/tasks/common/problemCollectors.ts#L359) to filter their pushes by the textModel opened/closed status, like here [if (shouldApplyMatch)](https://github.com/microsoft/vscode/blob/a5914335df0bf1cae7d818a168ef321def9f8572/src/vs/workbench/contrib/tasks/common/problemCollectors.ts#L392). So, problem matchers filter their outputs based on the **assumption** that there may be other marker provider active, to not mess with it. This mechanic is not bulletproof and may create more issues in the future if more marker providers appear, and this already creates issue in the scenario discussed there. So this is the first thing we change - we let marker providers push their data to markerService without collision preventing workarounds, by adding a `origin` tag in addition to `owner` and `resource`. `origin` entity is already added by @dbaeumer https://github.com/microsoft/vscode/issues/251268#issuecomment-3024704155, https://github.com/microsoft/vscode/pull/253368, and now we can take it to the more substantive usage with some adjustments. For now, `origin` is `string | undefined` and is set as string for the markers originated from extension host, and undefined for everything else.

So, the first is - we removing repushes of markers by `WatchingProblemCollector` on textModel dispose, and remove their outputs filtering based on textModel existence. Simply push any marker updates to `markerService`. This significantly simplifies the update logic for marker providers

Now, the essence of suggestion is `markerService` improvement to make it able to switch active origin (naming is under the question, it may be named `visible/presenting/facadeOrigin`,  but for now I just called it `activeOrigin`), which means that [MarkerService.read](https://github.com/microsoft/vscode/blob/a5914335df0bf1cae7d818a168ef321def9f8572/src/vs/platform/markers/common/markerService.ts#L332) called for `owner` and `resource` outputs only markers for active origin, and triggers [onMarkerChanged](https://github.com/microsoft/vscode/blob/a5914335df0bf1cae7d818a168ef321def9f8572/src/vs/platform/markers/common/markerService.ts#L158) event for updates of active origin markers only. Updates of other origins for the given owner+resource are still served, but they land to '`backyard`' storage, not visible in output and don't fire onMarkerChanged events

Thats it, it s actually simple idea. I may be unaware of impossibility of this change, but at a first glance, I like how it works. What do we get if we implement it:
1. Marker providers update pushes simplification
2. Markers storage is always up to date
3. Active origin switch is instant
4. Origin can be turned into more complex object with a hierarchy structure in the future, which may include origins prioritization logics. For example, for now we have only two priority levels - problem matchers (and maybe something else), for which we can leave origin as undefined for now, and a extension diagnostics level, which is more prioritized. There could be more levels between these two in the future, lets say we have a problem matcher diagnostics as a lowest one, then if there is some language service pushes markers it may have higher priority, and a language extension even more prioritized when a document is presented for editing. When document is removed from ui, markerService switch activeOrigin to another, language service in this case. If language service disappears, it switches to undefined origin, which is problem matchers atm. Probably too many words used to explain simple prioritization mechanics =)

I’m currently working on the implementation for pod-level resource limits defaulting, based on the guidance that pod-level limits should be derived from aggregated container limits **only when**:

1. Pod-level resource requests are explicitly set, and
2. All containers in the pod have resource limits set.

I’d like to clarify an edge case around what it means for *“all containers to have limits set”*.

Consider a pod with three containers:

* Container A sets a CPU limit but does **not** set a memory limit
* Container B sets a memory limit but does **not** set a CPU limit
* Container C sets both CPU and memory limits

In this situation, each resource dimension (CPU, memory) is covered by at least one container, but **no single container defines limits for all resources**.

My questions are:

* Should this pod be treated as *not having all container limits set*, and therefore **skip defaulting pod-level limits and return early**?
* Or should defaulting be evaluated **per resource dimension**, meaning we aggregate CPU limits from containers that define CPU limits and memory limits from containers that define memory limits?
* If the latter is intended, how should we treat containers that omit a specific resource limit — should they be assumed unbounded for that resource, or excluded from the aggregation?

I want to ensure the implementation aligns with the intent behind avoiding pods having access to “unknown” resources while still handling partial container specifications consistently.

Any clarification or pointers to prior discussions would be very helpful.

Looking at nginx Ingress, here is the information gather by my 'agent'...

Short answer: the controller does not special‑case, normalize, or reject IP addresses in the Ingress rule hosts. It passes the string through and renders it into NGINX’s server_name as-is. That has different outcomes for IPv4 vs IPv6.

What happens in code
- Host is taken verbatim into the Server object
  - controller.createServers(): rule.Host is copied into server.Hostname (empty -> "_") with no IP/DNS validation
    - file: internal/ingress/controller/controller.go
- The NGINX template renders server_name using that hostname unchanged (except for wildcard handling)
  - template: server_name {{ buildServerName $server.Hostname }} …
    - file: rootfs/etc/nginx/template/nginx.tmpl
  - buildServerName only rewrites wildcard names; otherwise returns the input string
    - file: internal/ingress/controller/template/template.go (buildServerName)
- Admission/safety checks do not reject IP hosts
  - inspector.CheckRegex() only blocks dangerous substrings (alias/root/etc); it does not validate DNS vs IP
    - file: internal/ingress/inspector/{ingress.go,rules.go}
- TLS certificate selection for such a host will use the host string
  - verifyHostname() treats IPs specially and only matches against IP SANs
    - file: internal/ingress/controller/certificate.go (verifyHostname)

Resulting behavior
- IPv4 host (e.g., 203.0.113.10)
  - NGINX gets: server_name 203.0.113.10; This is valid in NGINX and will match requests whose Host header is that IP.
  - TLS: the controller will associate a cert only if it has the IP in its SANs; otherwise it falls back to the default cert. Note many clients don’t send SNI for IP literals, so the default cert may be served at handshake time regardless.
- IPv6 host (e.g., 2001:db8::1)
  - NGINX would be rendered with: server_name 2001:db8::1; Colons aren’t valid in server_name tokens. On reload, the controller runs nginx -t (testTemplate in internal/ingress/controller/nginx.go); nginx -t will fail, so the reload is aborted and the previous (last good) config stays active.

Bottom line
- The controller accepts and forwards IP hosts unchanged.
- IPv4 literal hosts work (host-based vhost keyed to the IP in the Host header); TLS requires an IP SAN to avoid cert mismatch. 
- IPv6 literal hosts cause an invalid NGINX configuration and prevent reload.

Note: Per Kubernetes networking.k8s.io/v1 spec, Ingress .spec.rules[].host is a DNS name. Most clusters will reject IPs at API validation, so you typically can’t create such Ingresses. The above describes what the controller does if it nevertheless receives one (e.g., older API/validation gap).
IPv6 is not a valid 'domain name' anyway though, so it would still not pass the domain name validation, and just not be supported.

Here is the info about the Gateway behavior: in short, the IP V4 would get through, but is not supposed to be supported.
I will test behavior with Envoy Gateway provider as a started and see what happens, but Gateway may also need some formal modification to support this fully.

> Short answer:
> - Not supported. Gateway API Hostname fields explicitly disallow IP literals. That applies to both IPv4 and IPv6.
> - IPv6 literals will be rejected by schema validation (fail fast at admission) because the Hostname regex only allows DNS labels (no colons/brackets).
> - IPv4 literals are also disallowed by spec; however, the regex used for Hostname matches RFC1123 labels and can accept something that looks like 10.0.0.1. Although such values may be admitted by the API server, they are non-conformant and behavior is implementation-specific. Do not rely on them.
> 
> What the code and CRDs say:
> - apis/v1/shared_types.go: Hostname string
>   • Comment: “IPs are not allowed.”
>   • Validation: Pattern ^(\*\.)?[a-z0-9]([-a-z0-9]*[a-z0-9])?(\.[a-z0-9]([-a-z0-9]*[a-z0-9])?)*$
> - apis/v1/httproute_types.go (and grpc/tls routes): Hostname/hostnames fields repeat “IPs are not allowed.”
> - Listener.hostname is also Hostname (same regex and rule; config/crd/.../gateways.yaml has XValidations using the same pattern). 
> - TLSRoute SNI hostnames: CRD descriptions explicitly state “IPs are not allowed in SNI names per RFC 6066.”
> - PreciseHostname (used e.g., for HTTPRequestRedirect.hostname and some response rewriting): comment says numeric IP addresses are not allowed with its own pattern.
> 
> Expected behavior by case:
> - HTTPRoute.spec.hostnames or GRPCRoute.spec.hostnames set to an IPv6 literal (e.g., [2001:db8::1], or 2001:db8::1): rejected at admission with a pattern-validation error. This is a graceful, early failure.
> - Listener.hostname set to IPv6 literal: same, rejected at admission.
> - Any field typed as PreciseHostname set to IP (v4 or v6): rejected at admission.
> - HTTPRoute/GRPCRoute hostnames set to IPv4 literal (e.g., 10.0.0.1): spec says “IPs are not allowed”, but the regex can admit this because RFC1123 permits numeric labels. If admitted, it’s non-conformant; controllers are not required to support it. Possible outcomes are implementation-specific: some may ignore/mismatch; others may match literally; status conditions like NoMatchingListenerHostname could appear depending on the controller’s handling. There is no guarantee.
> 
> Guidance and workarounds:
> - Don’t use IPs in Hostname/hostnames anywhere in Gateway API routing rules. Use DNS names.
> - If you need to accept requests addressed to the Gateway IP (client sends Host: 10.0.0.1), leave Listener.hostname and Route hostnames unset so they match all hostnames; route by path/headers instead. You cannot explicitly match the IP literal via hostnames in a conformant way.
> - For fields that describe external origins/URIs (e.g., CORSOrigin, AbsoluteURI), IP hosts are allowed, but those are not used for hostname routing intersection; they are separate features.
> 
> Bottom line:
> - IPv4 and IPv6 IPs are not supported as Gateway routing hostnames. IPv6 is always rejected by schema; IPv4 may pass schema but is still out-of-spec and behavior is controller-dependent. Prefer DNS names or leave hostnames empty to match all.

Hmm, this still shows at least a concurrency issue in our tests that could be triggered. I think that warrants a fix at minimum. 

> Without this artificial delay, the initialization completes before any other code can interact with the locks.

Are we sure about this? While it seems unlikely that this can happen, I looked through the traces and spotted some concerning sections with the sleep that @user12031 showed.

The run lock is trying to be acquired by the `run` function and the distribute function is being called by `processReplacedListInfo` in `controller.go`. This does seem like it can happen in a real scenario, however unlikely it is.

```
	defer wg.Wait()                                         // Wait for Processor to stop
	defer stopProcessor(errors.New("informer is stopping")) // Tell Processor to stop
	// TODO: extend the MutationDetector interface so that it optionally
	// has a RunWithContext method that we can use here.
	wg.StartWithChannel(processorStopCtx.Done(), s.cacheMutationDetector.Run)
	wg.StartWithContext(processorStopCtx, s.processor.run)

	defer func() {
		s.startedLock.Lock()
		defer s.startedLock.Unlock()
		s.stopped = true // Don't want any new listeners
	}()
	s.controller.RunWithContext(ctx)
```

Due to the fact that wg.Wait only pauses after `s.controller.RunWithContext(ctx)` starts up is a bit of a concern. This seems like the root cause of the issue, since the controller will eventually trigger a replace which adds elements to the informer before it is started, strange...

Since this hasn't been reported on a live env, it seems likely that the informer starts up far quicker than the controller starts pushing events, but I agree that this looks like a real deadlock, possibly worse than just a goroutine leak. I think the main reason we don't see this is that the controller starting a watch is a far greater magnitude of time than the startup time of an informer.

  Goroutine 24 - User: ./staging/src/k8s.io/apimachinery/pkg/watch/mux.go:268 k8s.io/apimachinery/pkg/watch.(*Broadcaster).loop (0xb0207f) [chan receive]
  Goroutine 25 - User: ./staging/src/k8s.io/client-go/tools/cache/shared_informer.go:1024 k8s.io/client-go/tools/cache.(*processorListener).add (0xfb2549) [chan send]
  Goroutine 27 - User: /nvme/gopath/go-1.25.2/src/runtime/sema.go:100 sync.runtime_SemacquireRWMutexR (0x48be05) [wait for GC cycle]
  Goroutine 28 - User: /nvme/gopath/go-1.25.2/src/sync/mutex.go:46 sync.(*Mutex).Lock (0x4a233f) [trace reader (blocked)]
  Goroutine 29 - User: /nvme/gopath/go-1.25.2/src/runtime/sema.go:114 sync.runtime_SemacquireWaitGroup (0x48bece) [preempted]
* Goroutine 32 - User: /nvme/gopath/go-1.25.2/src/runtime/sema.go:105 sync.runtime_SemacquireRWMutex (0x48be65) [GC worker (idle)]
```

- 32 in sharedProcessor.shouldResync tries to lock `p.listenersLock`, called by `startResync`
- 29 in watchWithResync waits for 32 to stop
- 28 in RealFIFO.Close tries to lock f.lock
- 27 in sharedProcessor.run tries to lock p.listenersLock before starting the listeners (this is what got delayed)
- 25 in processorListener.add tries to write to p.addCh
- 24 in Broadcaster.loop tries to read m.incoming

So who holds `p.listenersLock`? It's goroutine 25, holding the lock in sharedProcessor.distribute while being blocked during event delivery.

So it seems the problem is that sharedProcessor.distribute assumes that sharedProcessor.run has started all listeners, but prevents that from happening when reached to soon.

I wonder whether `sharedProcessor.distribute` should check that all listeners have been started. If not, yield the mutex and wait on a condition. Code starting the listeners must signal that mutex.

Yep, my thought as well. Let me see if there's an easy way to handle this from distribute. Otherwise, we may have to wait to call `s.controller.RunWithContext(ctx)` until the listeners are started inside of the run function.
Perhaps tracking "started" for each listener is overkill. The global `p.listenersStarted` might be good enough because `sharedProcessor.addListener` will not block while holding the mutex.

some musings:
first and foremost, this small enhancement seems reasonnable and useful to me. I agree it would be good to have it.

next, I'd also prefer kubelet to set the values because the current model is kubelet owning the node and the cgroup management of pods (with everything else built upon that).
I'm advocating since quite some time to start thinking about how the kubelet can delegate these responsabilities to other components, like a [CPU DRA driver](https://github.com/kubernetes-sigs/dra-driver-cpu), so why prefer kubelet owning this setting? Because I think the best path is for the community to agree and design a proper delegation model rather than go piecewise following specific issues, because this creates a fragmented space harder to integrate later on and an explosion of special conditions, which we have plenty already. The path should be _conceptually_ like docker -> CRI we did in the quite distant past (and we can totally start with a small well defined core and iterate later on).

So, kubelet should own it only if the kernel supports it, which seems fair so far. Next question would be if use should control it or not (e.g. emergency disable). I think defaulting to this behavior seems the most user-friendly choice and an emergency disable FG seems the best approach.

Which made me think if this work deserves a small KEP because we're actually doing all the things the KEP process mandates, but informally here: thinking about integration parts, impacts on the ecosystem, UX flow, failure modes...

1. Expected positive impact (design objective)

a:cpu.idle, Permission problem or the cgroup controller is not attached: log error, BestEffort cgroup configuration failure
The more difficult problem is:

@ffromani Hi， I saw this PR today. According to your question, I have a deep look at the code, and I answer your question. There may be some mistakes, which can be corrected:
1. According to the code tracking, the main concurrency sources in the call tree of kubelet are:
A: Pod Scope Administration of Topology Manager (serial but different pods can be concurrent)
Call chain:
TopologyManager.Admit() -> calculateAffinity() -> allocateAlignedResources() -> provider.Allocate(pod, container)  ->DeviceManager.Allocate() 
All containers of a single pod call allocateAlignedResources serially. However, different pods can enter the administration process concurrently. There is no global lock to protect the Allocate calls between different pods
B: Reallocation in SyncPod process (concurrent with administration)

There are multiple issues here, lets split them:

1) On gang scheduling semantics for LWS vs Deployment. The Workload api doesn't specify how gang scheduling is applied to a specific "deployment" api (LWS, Deployment, StatefulSet etc.), it is more about how one sets the selectors. If one sets the selectors to define a gang as pods in a Deployment, then that Deployment's pods will be gang scheduled. For cases like LWS, which defines groups of pods as replicas, then the workload api also gives the ability to define "replicated gangs". So I don't believe there is inconsistency.

2) On minCount, this is specific to gang scheduling of pods (pods specifically, not "replicas", as in not LWS replicas, only pods within the gang) that should be scheduled in an all-or-nothing manner. Management of individual replicas, whether the replica is a group of pods (in LWS case) or individual pods (in Deployment case), is a separate matter from gang scheduling. 

3) On minCount and the lack of guarantees for the leader, I indeed think this is a gap, but it should be possible to amend the api 
to take this case into account. Great catch!

4) On managing groups of replicas (for example at least x prefill and y decode), whether a replica is a pod or a group of pods, this is not looked at as a gang-scheduling (all-or-nothing) problem per se; k8s has an API called PodDisruptionBudget (PDB), admittedly the name is legacy and is focused on Pods, but there is an effort to change that to give it "Replica Disruption Budget" semantics so that we can apply the concept on application apis like LWS. However, as you mention in the second gap, I agree that we should revisit this and discuss if scheduling policies across replicas is a concept that we want to bring to the new Workload api, keep it in PDB or propose a third api.   

  The current gang-scheduling capability in the workload api (which again is pod-centric) covers some of this for the single-node case only because for single-node a replica is a pod, not because it is intentionally trying to support it for single-node and not for multi-node.

Just to summarize my thoughts, I am aligned on addressing the two gaps, specifically: 

1) Allow specifying that the leader in a gang is a must to schedule even when a minCount is set
2) Defining inter-replica scheduling policies, whether by expanding the workload api to capture those policies or via PDB

I agree that this should ultimately be addressed by a gang-of-gangs abstraction, but I am concerned that an initial implementation may not fully meet the requirements. A natural first approach to gang-of-gangs is to treat each component (e.g., prefill-leader, prefill-worker, decode-leader, decode-worker) as contributing to a single top-level gang with a set of aggregate minCount constraints (for example, at least one prefill leader and one group of three prefill workers), while still maintaining the existing per-component minCount semantics (e.g., prefill workers scheduled in groups of three).

While this model is sufficient for initial placement, it becomes limiting once scaling is introduced. In particular, it does not provide a clear way to express which components must be gang-scheduled together versus which can scale independently. For example, when scaling both prefill and decode, we typically want prefill leaders and prefill workers to be scheduled as a unit, without being blocked by an inability to schedule additional decode leaders. A flat top-level gang constraint risks coupling unrelated components during scaling, leading to unnecessary scheduling stalls.

 Aside: The difficulties of concisely and clearly encoding these types of constraints while retaining familiar k8s workflows like scaling and rolling updates into resources like Deployment or LeaderWorkerSet are why we built Grove, but Grove is fundamentally still an intent-layer. To be able to provide the full functionality using default kube-scheduler it would need Workload API to support richer semantics around gang-scheduling and eventually topology aware scheduling.

I talked to a kernel nftables hacker (Florian) and he confirmed that this is the "check that there are no loops" code. (When adding new rules or verdict map elements, it needs to confirm that all `jump`s/`goto`s only go to chains you haven't hit yet, so there can't be loops.) Coincidentally, he was actually just working on this code (https://lore.kernel.org/netfilter-devel/20251126114703.8826-1-fw@strlen.de/) and said he'll send a slightly improved version of that patch soon. But he also confirmed there's no way to fix this with existing kernels other than "have fewer jumps/chains".

We had talked before about squashing the endpoint chains into the service chains; instead of doing

```
add rule ip kube-proxy service-LAUZTJTB-ns4/svc4/tcp/p80
  numgen random mod 2 vmap {
    0 : goto endpoint-UNZV3OEC-ns4/svc4/tcp/p80__10.180.0.4/80 ,
    1 : goto endpoint-5RFCDDV7-ns4/svc4/tcp/p80__10.180.0.5/80
  }
```

it would just do

```
add rule ip kube-proxy service-LAUZTJTB-ns4/svc4/tcp/p80
  numgen random mod 2 vmap {
    0 : meta l4proto tcp dnat to 10.180.0.4:80 ,
    1 : meta l4proto tcp dnat to 10.180.0.5:80
  }
```

The problem with this is that the endpoint chain doesn't _just_ do DNAT; it also does masquerade-if-hairpin and, potentially, affinity. Affinity is sort of complicated, but it doesn't apply to most services, so we could just ignore that for now ("ignore" = "don't change the rule structure for services using affinity"). So, given that, if we could redo the hairpin handling to not need endpoint-specific rules, then we could get rid of the endpoint chains in _most_ cases. And I guess we could do that with a post-dnat dummy map:

```
add rule ip kube-proxy service-LAUZTJTB-ns4/svc4/tcp/p80
  ip saddr . ip daddr vmap {
    10.180.0.4 . 10.180.0.4 : jump mark-for-masquerade ,
    10.180.0.5 . 10.180.0.5 : jump mark-for-masquerade
  }
```

I guess it would be better if we eliminated the `jump` here too. `mark-for-masquerade` just does `mark set mark or 0x4000`, but we can't put that into a vmap.... I guess we could just squash all of the hairpin handling into a single map lookup in `services` rather than having per-service hairpin handling...

On the `nft` issues, this is a topic Dan and I commented several times, should we use `nft` userspace or should we use `netlink` interface directly?

The main tradeoff is complexity to gain performance and also to reduce userspace dependencies (you can use distroless images so security fixes and image updates are only related to golang)

I started moving some of the projects completely to the netlink format and also documented the process in https://github.com/kubernetes-sigs/kindnet/blob/main/docs/nftables-netlink.md

- https://github.com/kubernetes-sigs/kube-network-policies/pull/136
- https://github.com/aojea/kindnet/pull/139

As you can see, is way simpler to use Dan's library https://github.com/kubernetes-sigs/knftables , but at the cost of shelling out and having to delegate to `nft` all the preprocessing. On the contrary, we need to implement all the preprocessing in golang to generate the corresponding bytecode ...

I think that if we are targeting this scale, we can open a KEP to move kube-proxy nftables to netlink , so we can remove one of the bottlenecks that is `nft`

Note that switching to netlink would not help with the kernel side of this bug, which is solely about how many chains and jumps you have, not about how you create them.

However, it would likely help with the "nft using lots of CPU" part (which is unrelated to the kernel softlock).

> I guess we could just squash all of the hairpin handling into a single map lookup in `services` rather than having per-service hairpin handling...

(of course if we switch to raw netlink then we don't even need a map; the nftables bytecode lets you write a rule that does "if source IP equals dest IP", there's just no way to express that in the high-level nftables language.)
